hints: Look at the three shapes carefully and ask yourself which element can exist in all these different forms.
Notice that P shows flat hexagonal layers and Q shows a 3D tetrahedral network, both classic extended lattices of carbon.
Compare those endless repeating networks with R, which is a closed hollow ball made of a fixed number of atoms that exists as a separate molecule.
walkthrough:
**Identify the element and its allotropes**

Great spot, all three diagrams are different forms of carbon. P is graphite with its flat hexagonal layers, Q is diamond with its tetrahedral 3D framework, and R is a fullerene ($\text{C}_{60}$) shaped like a hollow football.

**Recall what giant molecular means**

A giant molecular (also called giant covalent) structure is an endless 3D or 2D network of atoms joined by covalent bonds.

Rule to use:
$$\text{giant} = \text{continuous lattice with no discrete molecules}$$

**Classify P, Q and R**

P (graphite) has covalent bonds extending throughout each huge layer, so it is giant. Q (diamond) has every carbon bonded tetrahedrally in a continuous 3D lattice, so it is also giant. R ($\text{C}_{60}$) is different, it is a discrete molecule with a fixed number of atoms held to other molecules only by weak forces, so it is simple molecular, not giant.

options.A: Incorrect. While P and Q are giant networks, R is not. R is buckminsterfullerene, $\text{C}_{60}$, which exists as separate closed molecules, so it is simple molecular.
options.B: Correct. P is graphite and Q is diamond. Both are continuous covalent lattices with no molecular boundaries, so both are giant molecular. R is excluded because it is a discrete fullerene molecule.
options.C: Incorrect. P is correctly included as giant, but R should not be. Students sometimes think the large ball must be giant because it looks big, but it contains only 60 carbons and acts as one molecule.
options.D: Incorrect. Q is correctly included as giant, but R should not be and P is wrongly left out. P (graphite) is a giant layered structure even though the layers are held by weak forces, the covalent bonding within each layer is continuous.
